Title: Louise Erdrich
Chunks: 8,9,10,11,12
In 1995, their son Sava accused Dorris of committing child abuse.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Erdrich#cite_note-23) Dorris and Erdrich separated in 1995,[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Erdrich#cite_note-dorris-9) and divorced in 1996.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Erdrich#cite_note-divorceandaccusations-11) In 1997, after Dorris's death by suicide, his adopted daughter Madeline claimed that Dorris had sexually abused her also and that Erdrich had neglected to stop the abuse.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Erdrich#cite_note-:3-24)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Erdrich#cite_note-dorrisaccused-10)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Erdrich#cite_note-dorris-9) Dorris's will omitted Erdrich, Sava, and Madeline.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Erdrich#cite_note-:3-24)

In 2001, at age 47, Erdrich gave birth to a daughter, Azure, whose Native American father Erdrich declines to identify publicly.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Erdrich#cite_note-25) She discusses her pregnancy with Azure, and Azure's father, in her 2003 nonfiction book, _Books and Islands in Ojibwe Country_.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Erdrich#cite_note-:4-26) She uses the name "Tobasonakwut" to refer to him.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Erdrich#cite_note-:5-27)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Erdrich#cite_note-28) He is described as a traditional healer and teacher, who is eighteen years Erdrich's senior and a married man.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Erdrich#cite_note-:5-27)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Erdrich#cite_note-:4-26) In a number of publications, Tobasonakwut Kinew, who died in 2012, is referred to as Erdrich's partner and the father of Azure.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Erdrich#cite_note-29)
When asked in an interview if writing is a lonely life for her, Erdrich replied, "Strangely, I think it is. I am surrounded by an abundance of family and friends and yet I am alone with the writing. And that is perfect." Erdrich lives in [Minneapolis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minneapolis "Minneapolis").[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Erdrich#cite_note-Interview-30)

In 1979, she wrote "The World's Greatest Fisherman",[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Erdrich#cite_note-31) a short story about June Kashpaw, a divorced Ojibwe woman whose death by [hypothermia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hypothermia "Hypothermia") brought her relatives home to a fictional North Dakota reservation for her funeral. She wrote this while "barricaded in the kitchen."[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Erdrich#cite_note-:0-15) At her husband's urging, she submitted it to the Nelson Algren Short Fiction competition in 1982, where it won the $5,000 prize.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Erdrich#cite_note-:0-15) It later became the first chapter of her debut novel, _[Love Medicine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love\_Medicine "Love Medicine")_, published by [Holt, Rinehart, and Winston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holt,_Rinehart,_and_Winston "Holt, Rinehart, and Winston") in 1984.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Erdrich#cite_note-Interview-30)
"When I found out about the prize I was living on a farm in New Hampshire near the college I'd attended," Erdrich told an interviewer. "I was nearly broke and driving a car with bald tires. My mother knitted my sweaters, and all else I bought at thrift stores ... The recognition dazzled me. Later, I became friends with [Studs Terkel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Studs_Terkel "Studs Terkel") and [Kay Boyle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kay_Boyle "Kay Boyle"), the judges, toward whom I carry a lifelong gratitude. This prize made an immense difference in my life."[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Erdrich#cite_note-32)

_Love Medicine_ won the 1984 National Book Critics Circle Award.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Erdrich#cite_note-Author:_Louise_Erdrich-33) It is the only debut novel ever to receive that honor.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Erdrich#cite_note-34) Erdrich later turned _Love Medicine_ into a tetralogy that includes _The Beet Queen_ (1986), _[Tracks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tracks\_(novel) "Tracks (novel)")_ (1988), and _[The Bingo Palace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Bingo\_Palace "The Bingo Palace")_ (1994). It has also been featured on the National [Advanced Placement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Advanced_Placement "Advanced Placement") Test for Literature.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Erdrich#cite_note-35)
In the early years of their marriage, Erdrich and Michael Dorris often collaborated on their work, saying they plotted the books together, "talk about them before any writing is done, and then we share almost every day, whatever it is we've written" but "the person whose name is on the books is the one who's done most of the primary writing."[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Erdrich#cite_note-:1-20) They got started with "domestic, romantic stuff" published under the shared pen name of "Milou North" (Michael + Louise + where they live).[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Erdrich#cite_note-:0-15)

During the publication of _Love Medicine_, Erdrich produced her first collection of poems, _Jacklight_ (1984), which highlights the struggles between Native and non-Native cultures, as well as celebrating family, ties of kinship, autobiographical meditations, monologues, and love poetry. She incorporates elements of Ojibwe myths and legends.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Erdrich#cite_note-Louise_Erdrich_2010-18) Erdrich continues to write poems, which have been included in her collections.
Erdrich is best known as a novelist, and has published a dozen award-winning and best-selling novels.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Erdrich#cite_note-Louise_Erdrich_2010-18) She followed _Love Medicine_ with _The Beet Queen_ (1986), which continued her technique of using [multiple narrators](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multiperspectivity "Multiperspectivity")[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Erdrich#cite_note-36) and expanded the fictional reservation universe of _Love Medicine_ to include the nearby town of Argus, North Dakota. The action of the novel takes place mostly before [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II"). [Leslie Marmon Silko](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leslie_Marmon_Silko "Leslie Marmon Silko") accused Erdrich's _The Beet Queen_ of being more concerned with [postmodern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Postmodern_literature "Postmodern literature") technique than with the political struggles of Native peoples.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Erdrich#cite_note-37)

Donna Fargo has an amazing run of hits including six country #1s. In 1978 came hard news. She was diagnosed with multiple sclerosis. With that diagnosis, Fargo started setting major goals. She's taking on a new goal just for America 250.
![Image 1: Donna Fargo talks new book, MS, and gift she wants to give new citizens](https://ewscripps.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/880236e/2147483647/strip/false/crop/1280x714+0+3/resize/95x53!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fcf.cdn.uplynk.com%2Fause1%2Fslices%2F7ef%2F9ca48a3b38ef42538c6fe52a659b1e99%2F7ef1a541c131441fb7287523f4caaff8%2Fposter_d1893e7005714e84816c61dc00440d5c.jpeg)
![Image 2: Donna Fargo](https://ewscripps.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/055de94/2147483647/strip/true/crop/1280x720+0+0/resize/1280x720!/quality/90/?url=http%3A%2F%2Fewscripps-brightspot.s3.amazonaws.com%2F7a%2Fbf%2F406376c142ce822cd37dd536d61a%2Ffargo-one.jpg)
NASHVILLE, Tenn. (WTVF) — Always a writer. That's the story of Donna Fargo.
It was the early 70s. Fargo was an English teacher in California when she took a trip to Tennessee with Stan Silver.
"Stan was my manager, producer, love of my life, husband," Fargo said.
The trip was to Nashville to record a few songs.

"I didn't know any writers, so I thought, 'mm. I bet I could write my own," she continued.
Among those songs was something she'd first called The Happiest Girl in the World.
"I knew I had to rhyme with world," Fargo remembered. "It's a more cumbersome rhyme scheme."
She thought maybe something else would rhyme better.
"It just came out. I'm The Happiest Girl in the Whole USA," Fargo nodded.
The song was Fargo's breakthrough. A country and pop crossover hit. What followed was incredible honors and accolades. For the six years following 1972, Fargo had 16 country top tens, six of which were number ones. Nearly all of them were songs she'd written herself.
"I didn't plan it that way!" Fargo said. "I just didn't know any writers! Ha! I was just blessed to the bone."
It was all amazing for that high school English teacher.
In 1978 came very hard news. Fargo was diagnosed with multiple sclerosis.
"You're a prisoner in your own body," she said. "I have full body numbness from it. I have a lot of body misery from MS and two strokes, and I know that drives me. When your mind is occupied, you can zone out the misery in your body."
Since 1978, Fargo has set constant goals, always returning to her writing. She's just written and released a new song.
"Small Town Hillbilly Good Time Saturday Night!" Fargo said with a smile.
She's written books and more than 2,000 greeting cards. She often writes about her faith, and she's just released her first novel, Heartaches and Mindstorms.
"I'm working on another book now," Fargo added. "I don't know where it's going, but I trust the process."
Fargo has just set another goal unlike anything she's tried before.
In that run of country top 10s, Fargo had another song with USA in the title; 1974's US of A.
"I just love our country," Fargo said. "I've always felt like we're one big family."
What Fargo wants to do is give a copy of her song lyrics as a gift to new US citizens at naturalization ceremonies.

"To practice diligently an attitude of brotherly love and hold no hatred against anyone," Fargo said, reciting part of the song. "I will try to treat him as he'd want to be treated, with compassion and understanding."
Fargo said she's not sure how to get this done, but it's an interesting new journey.
"I've said before, yeah, I have MS, but it doesn't have me," Fargo said. "They're not gonna rule my life."
It's like I told you. Donna Fargo is a writer.

# John Gomez
## About the author
John Gomez (1967- ) lives in Minnesota, near the Twin Cities. He was born in Fargo, North Dakota, and has lived near and far. His series, "Molly's Adventures", provides an introductory tool for discussions for the young and their special people.
Growing up, John didn't have pets and, as a parent of two wonderful cats and an exceptional dog, he has daily merriment and adventures. He will continue to love these furry family members each day with their wondrous gifts.
If John can bring some of their light to others, he will continue to live in joy.
Generally, he can be reached at johngomez9999@gmail.com.
